title: Holocene extinction

definition.text: The ongoing wave of extinctions of plants and animals, on land and at sea, caused by human activity in the current geological epoch.

facts.text: It is sometimes called the sixth extinction, and when the stress falls on human causes it is also called the Anthropocene extinction.
Species are now estimated to be disappearing 100 to 1,000 times faster than the natural background extinction rate.

Its drivers include climate change, destruction of wetlands, deforestation, overfishing, ocean acidification, population growth, economic growth and rising consumption, especially in affluent societies.
Scientists broadly agree that habitat destruction, resource consumption and the elimination of species are the main human drivers of the crisis.
The 2019 IPBES Global Assessment estimated that about one million species are at risk of extinction within decades because of human activities.
A 2023 study counted at least 73 animal genera lost since 1500, a rate it judged 35 times higher than the background rate without human impacts.
Population growth, economic growth and growth in consumption per person over the past two centuries are regarded as its underlying causes.
Proposed remedies include shifting economic activity toward low-impact sectors, plant-based diets, and enlarging protected areas on land and sea.

related: Global Assessment Report on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services

title: Sixth mass extinction debate

definition.text: The scientific argument over whether today's human-caused extinctions already amount to a mass extinction like the five great ones in the fossil record.

facts.text: A mass extinction is defined as the loss of at least 75% of species within a geologically short period of less than 2 million years.
Some researchers call recent losses dramatic and serious but not yet a mass extinction in the palaeontological sense of the Big Five.
Others, including a 2022 review in Biological Reviews, argue that a sixth mass extinction caused by human activity is already under way.
Estimates of species lost per year range widely, from 1.5 to 40,000, but all point to human activity as the cause.

contested_note: Scientists disagree on whether current extinction rates already qualify as a mass extinction or only threaten one.

title: Human role in megafaunal extinctions

definition.text: The question of how far hunting by spreading human populations, rather than a changing climate, caused large animals to die out at the end of the last ice age.

facts.text: Megafaunal extinctions correlate with the arrival of humans, and human activity has been the main cause of mammal extinctions since the Late Pleistocene.
Worldwide, 178 species of the largest mammals died out between 52,000 and 9,000 BC.
A rival theory holds that climate change near the end of the Pleistocene stressed megafauna to extinction; some scientists think hunting and climate acted together.
Africa lost the fewest megafauna, possibly because its animals evolved alongside humans and learned to fear them.

contested_note: Sources disagree on how much human hunting, versus climate change, drove prehistoric megafaunal extinctions.

definition.text: The global crash of frog and salamander populations, driven partly by a fungal disease spread by human travel and the wildlife trade.

facts.text: Chytridiomycosis has caused severe declines in over 500 amphibian species and perhaps 90 extinctions.
Amphibians are now the most endangered vertebrate group, though they survived three earlier mass extinctions over more than 300 million years.
Amphibian decline is treated as an indicator of environmental degradation.

definition.text: A species introduced by people to a new place, where it harms the environment it has entered.

facts.text: Invasive species are the subset of established non-native species that threaten native species and biodiversity.
Invasions happen naturally, but human-assisted introductions have greatly increased their rate, scale and geographic range.
Biological invasion is one of the five top drivers of global biodiversity loss and is growing with tourism and globalization.
Common traits of invaders include fast growth, rapid reproduction, association with humans and earlier successful invasions.
An introduced species usually has to persist at low densities first, sometimes needing several introductions before it establishes.
Scientific consensus holds that their effects on biodiversity are mainly negative, though some can provide habitat or food for other organisms.
The term "invasive" is poorly defined and often subjective.

title: Economic costs of invasive species

definition.text: The money lost to damage from invasive species and spent on controlling them.

facts.text: The economic impact of invasive species was estimated to exceed $423 billion a year as of 2019.
This cost has quadrupled every decade since 1970.
Costs split into direct production losses in farming and forestry and the costs of management.
Counting only lost production and management understates the cost; valuing lost species and ecosystem services would raise it sharply.
Estimated damage and control costs in the United States exceed $138 billion a year.
In France, damage costs were nearly eight times higher than spending on management.
Invasive trees can bring benefits such as commercial forestry, but returns from invasive species are usually far smaller than their costs.
Early detection and rapid response is often called the key to management, but it helps only when reintroduction is rare and response is affordable.

notes: S:0243ea2eff9a gives global management expenditures of about $1.4 trillion a year, far above the $423 billion impact estimate in S:ea4de4ef05ec; the two figures measure different things or one may be wrong, so check before using either alongside the other.

definition.text: The routes, mostly human, by which non-native species are carried to new places.

facts.text: Humans carry organisms faster and farther than natural range expansion, both deliberately and by accident.
Repeated traffic, such as ships between ports, creates recurring chances for arrival and establishment, called high propagule pressure.
A 2008 study found shipping, through hull fouling and ballast water, to be the dominant pathway for marine invasive species.
Deliberate biocontrol introductions can backfire: about 100 cane toads brought to Australia have become over 200 million.

definition.text: Inspection and quarantine rules on traded goods and ships that aim to stop pests and invasive species crossing borders.

facts.text: The first global standards, including the WTO's Sanitary and Phytosanitary (SPS) Agreement, were agreed in 1994 to block agricultural pests while allowing farm exports.
The International Maritime Organization oversees the Ballast Water Management Convention.
The Convention on Biological Diversity is the most significant international agreement on invasive species, but most of its measures are voluntary and unspecific.

definition.text: Ecological restoration applied to islands, chiefly by removing introduced species and bringing back native ones.

facts.text: Islands hold many of the world's endemic species but are very vulnerable to introduced species because of their small size.
A 2019 study found that eradicating invasive animals on just 169 islands would improve survival prospects for 9.4% of the most highly threatened island vertebrates.

definition.text: Introducing a non-native species on purpose to fill an ecological role left empty by an extinct native species.

facts.text: On islets off Mauritius, Aldabra giant tortoises introduced in 2000 and 2007 are replacing extinct native tortoises as seed dispersers and grazers of invasive plants.

definition.text: A standardized questionnaire that scores how likely a plant is to cause harm in a new environment, before it is introduced.

facts.text: Predicting plant impacts is especially useful because most plant introductions are intentional.
The total score is tied to a management action such as "prevent introduction".

definition.text: A genetic-engineering technique that makes a chosen gene spread through a population faster than normal inheritance, proposed for wiping out invasive animals.

facts.text: It has been proposed as a way to eliminate invasive mammals in New Zealand.
Normally offspring have a 50:50 chance of inheriting either version of a gene; a gene drive suppresses the unwanted version.

title: Critiques of the invasive species concept
article: Invasive species#Criticisms of the invasive species discourse

definition.text: Arguments that not all biological invasions are harmful and that the language of invasion misleads.

facts.text: An "effective invasion" is one where an alien species fills a vacant niche and joins local food webs without displacing natives.
Some scientists urge that species moving to escape a warming climate be treated as refugees rather than invaders.
Entomologist Chris D. Thomas argues most introduced species are neutral or beneficial, a minority view.

contested_note: A minority of scientists dispute the consensus that invasive species are mainly harmful and object to the term itself.
